stem: A 50-year-old female presents with a breast mass. Core biopsy shows invasive carcinoma, ER-negative, PR-negative, HER2-negative (triple-negative). One axillary lymph node is positive on biopsy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

opts.t: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical resection
Surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy

expl: Triple-negative cancer with a positive node is chemo-sensitive and aggressive → neoadjuvant chemotherapy first (shrinks tumour/nodes, tests response, may allow conservation), then surgery.

why.B: SLNB is for a clinically negative axilla; this node is biopsy-positive.

stem: A 65 year old female presented to the clinic with a breast mass, biopsy showed that it was ER positive. She has a history of bilateral breast radiation for Hodgkin's Lymphoma. What is the appropriate management?
expl: Breast conservation requires radiotherapy; previous chest/breast irradiation (mantle field for Hodgkin's) makes repeat RT unsafe → mastectomy. Neoadjuvant therapy is not needed for a simple ER+ tumour.

why.B: Lumpectomy without RT has high local recurrence.
why.D: Not indicated for this ER+ tumour.

stem: A 33 year old patient presented to the clinic with a breast mass, biopsy showed that it was ER negative, PR negative and HER2 positive. What is the appropriate treatment?
expl: HER2-positive, hormone-receptor-negative → anti-HER2 therapy (trastuzumab) with chemotherapy. Tamoxifen, letrozole and goserelin are endocrine drugs that need ER positivity.

stem: What is the reason for sentinel lymph node biopsy in surgical breast cancer?

opts.t: To guide the radiation therapy decision
Assess the extent of lymphatic involvement
To assess tumor staging and prognosis

expl: Sentinel lymph node biopsy samples the first draining node(s) to find out whether the axilla is involved — i.e. the extent of lymphatic spread — without a full axillary dissection.

why.A: Radiation decisions may follow, but that's not its purpose.
why.C: Staging is a consequence; the direct purpose is assessing nodal involvement.
why.D: Same — chemo decisions follow from the result.

stem: Female came to the ER with Recurrent breast cellulitis 5 times with no improvement with multiple antibiotics. What is the next best management?
expl: "Cellulitis" that keeps recurring despite antibiotics must be biopsied to exclude inflammatory breast cancer (dermal lymphatic invasion).

stem: Macrocalcifications DCIS management?
expl: DCIS (detected as calcifications) is treated with breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy) + radiotherapy, or mastectomy if extensive. Hormone replacement is contraindicated in breast cancer.

why.C: Wrong (endocrine THERAPY like tamoxifen can be added, not HRT).

stem: Breast mass ER and PR +ve Her2 -ve , retroareolar mass with nipple retraction and no lymph node involvement best management i did nor remember the choices Incomplete recall. The source supplies no choices or answer key.
expl: The recall gives no choices. A central tumour with nipple retraction can still be conserved by excising the nipple–areola complex; node-negative → SLNB; ER+ → hormonal therapy.
ansText: Central (retroareolar) lumpectomy removing the nipple–areola complex with clear margins + sentinel lymph-node biopsy + whole-breast radiotherapy (or mastectomy + SLNB), followed by endocrine therapy because it is ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative.

stem: patient with breast mass with benign looking lymph nodes ( clinically and radiologically) What is the best treatment option?

opts.t: Total mastectomy with lymph node dissection
Breast consevetive surgery with sentinel lymph node biopsy

expl: A clinically and radiologically negative axilla → breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy + RT) with sentinel lymph-node biopsy — avoids ALND morbidity.

why.D: Includes ALND — not for a negative axilla.

stem: A 95 years old lady with devastating comorbidities came with a long standing breast mass that is starting to ulcerate, biopsy showed ER&PR (almost 100% positive), her HER is -ve, low ki-67 (5%), Grade1, with no metastasis. T3N0M0. What is the most logical management option?
expl: A 95-year-old with devastating comorbidities and a strongly ER/PR-positive, low-grade, low-Ki-67 (luminal A) tumour → endocrine therapy alone (aromatase inhibitor/tamoxifen) controls it well without surgical risk.

stem: 55 year old female with 10 year history of diabetes and hypertension and breast cancer 5 years ago, presented complained of Neck pain for the past 3 weeks, she has no history of trauma and no fever. What is your next step in management?
expl: New, persistent back/neck pain in a patient with previous breast cancer = bone metastasis until proven otherwise → MRI of the spine (also shows cord compression).

stem: a 70 year old man presented with left breast ulcerating mass and enlarged left axillary lymph nodes, which of the following is an appropriate initial management?
expl: A man with an ulcerating breast mass and axillary nodes = male breast cancer until proven otherwise → triple assessment: mammogram (± US) then core biopsy. Excision first is wrong.

why.A: Part of the metastatic screen later.

stem: A 47 year old female complains of bilateral breast pain with tenderness on the upper outer quadrant of both breasts. They ordered a mammogram for her, what is the reason for ordering a mammogram?

opts.t: Mammogram can show details of the mass

expl: Mammography's key strength is showing microcalcifications (and their type) and architectural distortion — early signs of cancer/DCIS.

why.D: US/MRI characterise masses better in dense breasts.

stem: A 28 year old female complains of unilateral bloody discharge from the right breast. Which of the following investigations will you order for her?
expl: A young woman (dense breasts) with bloody discharge → ultrasound first (retroareolar papilloma), then biopsy if needed.

stem: BRCA1 is seen commonly with which cancer?
expl: BRCA1 mutations predispose mainly to breast (and ovarian) cancer.

stem: A 47-year-old female presenting to your clinic with a recent history of palpable breast mass, 3 cm in size. What is the next step in managing this patient after obtaining history and physical examination?

opts.t: Breast imaging followed by biopsy from the mass
Surgical removal of this mass and sending it for histopathology

expl: Triple assessment: history/exam → imaging (mammogram ± US) → image-guided core biopsy. Imaging comes before biopsy so the biopsy doesn't distort the images and is targeted.

why.D: Excision isn't the first diagnostic step.

stem: Most common type of Breast cancer?
expl: Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type) is the commonest breast cancer (~75–80%); lobular is second.

stem: scenario about Stage 3 breast cancer (involvement of skin) -in the scenario There is bloody discharge and central mass) , core biopsy showed : invasive ductal carcinoma. Three lymph nodes involved in the question was asking about the appropriate Management.
srcNote: (Breast Cancer) Source note (Final 433 F Q8 (p. 189)): Management of locally advanced disease: start with systemic (chemo or hormonal) then if tumour is downstaged go for surgery then radiotherapy. If not downstaged we give radiotherapy then surgery. (From Dr. Alqahtani's book)
expl: Locally advanced breast cancer (skin involvement, several nodes — stage III) → neoadjuvant systemic therapy first, then surgery (usually mastectomy + ALND) and radiotherapy.

why.C: Not suitable for stage III with skin involvement.

stem: Which of the following is the most common presentation of breast cancer in Saudi Arabia?
expl: Most breast cancers present as a painless lump (in Saudi Arabia often larger/later).

stem: A forty-year-old lady is coming to you with metastatic (brain and bone) triple negative right breast cancer. What is the most appropriate management option for this patient?

opts.t: Right mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection

expl: Source key D. Metastatic (brain + bone) triple-negative breast cancer is incurable; treatment intent is palliative. The doctor's notes say stage IV is treated mainly systemically (palliative chemotherapy), so chemotherapy is also defensible — breast surgery is not indicated.

why.C: Palliative chemotherapy — reasonable (doctor), but not the key.

stem: Scenario about breast cancer and the question was which of the following is the best initial step, options are:
srcNote: (Breast Cancer) The source does not provide the full clinical scenario.
expl: The first diagnostic step for a suspicious breast mass is core needle biopsy (histology, ER/PR/HER2). FNA gives cytology only; surgery and SLNB come after diagnosis and staging.

stem: Regarding breast cancer which ONE of the following is the single most important prognostic factor?

opts.t: Number of involved axillary lymph nodes

expl: The single most important prognostic factor in breast cancer is the axillary lymph-node status (number of involved nodes).

expl: Paget's disease of the nipple is an eczema-like change of the nipple that reflects an underlying breast carcinoma (in situ or invasive).
